problem: Prior interactive agents either rely on low-bandwidth feedback (rewards or actions) or learn to ask by mimicking human questions, which are not necessarily useful to the agent, and they cannot flexibly request and use rich information such as state descriptions, goal descriptions or subgoals.
motivation: Autonomous agents fail in unfamiliar environments and on new task specifications, while humans nearby can supply useful information. An agent that knows what to ask, grounded in its own uncertainty and its own policy, could turn tasks beyond its abilities into ones it can do without retraining.
key_idea: HARI: a POMDP-based framework in which an agent learns by RL an intention policy that chooses among information-seeking intentions (ask for current-state description, goal description, or subgoal) or acts, with a goal stack managing recursive subgoals, and the assistant's replies are fed directly as inputs to the execution policy.
insight: Different information types are useful in different contexts, and RL discovers this: subgoal requests grow ~3.5x in unseen environments versus unseen objects, goal requests happen once at step 1, and current-state requests decline over time. The learned policy beats a rule-based baseline matched on action counts (+7.1% on unseen env), and an uncooperative assistant that ignores the requested intention degrades performance, so the gains come from making the right kind of request. Deeper goal stacks help unseen environments (+11.9% at size 3) but the critic overestimates the value of subgoal actions, so the agent over-requests subgoals.
method: Assistant model: an ever-present assistant knows the agent's state, the goal and the optimal policy, and can describe states (rho_A) and propose subgoals (omega_A).

Listener via description inputs: assistant replies are state or goal descriptions that go directly into the execution policy's input, so the protocol is as rich as the policy's input space; replies are appended to the history or replace the goal description.
Information-seeking intentions: the intention policy's action space is {cur-state request, goal request, subgoal request, do (execute the argmax action of the execution policy), done}.

Goal stack in the intention environment: a POMDP whose state includes a stack of at most L (goal, description) pairs; the goal request replaces the top description, the subgoal request pushes, and done pops.
Cost design with reward shaping: constant cost per request and per do action, task error (shortest-path distance) on done for the main goal, and potential-based shaping using the task error Phi.
Intention policy training: an LSTM actor and critic trained with A2C on top of the frozen pre-trained execution policy, whose hidden features and action distribution are its inputs.

Execution policy: V&L BERT-style Transformer pre-trained with DAgger on dense descriptions with random feature dropping; simulated human-assisted navigation on Matterport3D graphs with bag-of-features dense/sparse descriptions.

setting.backbone: Transformer execution policy (V&L BERT style, frozen after DAgger pre-training) + LSTM actor-critic intention policy trained with A2C
setting.model_size: execution policy hidden size 256, 2 layers, 8 heads; intention policy LSTM hidden 512
setting.training_data: Simulated data on Matterport3D graphs: 82,104 pre-training, 65,133 intention-policy training examples (36 environments for pre-training, 18 more unseen environments for training); no external data
setting.observation: Discrete bag-of-features descriptions (room name, up to 20 objects with distance and direction), dense or sparse; no images
setting.action_space: Discrete: move to adjacent nav-graph nodes; intention-level actions {cur, goal, subgoal request, do, done}
setting.simulator: Matterport3D simulator house layout graphs (simulated human-assisted navigation)
setting.privileged: Simulated assistant knows agent state, goal and shortest-path oracle; it gives dense descriptions and subgoals along the shortest path at test time (part of the interaction protocol)

results: With the learned intention policy, success rate rises about 2x on unseen start, 5x on unseen object and 7x on unseen environment versus no assistance (3.0 -> 19.8 on unseen env). It beats the rule-based dense-goal-and-state baseline in unseen environments (9.4) and the action-count-matched random+rules baseline (12.7). Only about 1/4 of its actions are requests.
limitations: Evaluated only in a simplified simulated setting with discrete bag-of-features descriptions and a scripted, always-cooperative assistant; generalization to real humans and raw perception is untested.
The execution policy is frozen and the agent does not learn from the information it receives; the intentions are only three generic types.
The critic is not expressive enough to represent stack configurations, so it overestimates subgoal values and over-requests with deeper stacks.
compares_to: Random policy with matched action counts
